text.en: The camp of Israel in the desert, seen from above with ruach hakodesh, was itself a Sefer Torah, with Levi in the middle like Vayikra among the five Chumashim.
The megadef's two complaints, about the camp and about the lechem hapanim, are one: if the loaves are cold, Hashem's love for Dan has cooled and Dan can take in an outsider.
The claim that Hashem's love for the Jews has cooled and passed to others is, according to the Rav, the whole teaching of Yeshu, the later incarnation of the megadef according to the Arizal.
The twelve loaves match the twelve distinct arrangements of Hashem's four-letter Name, since its two identical letters reduce twenty-four to twelve, so each tribe has its own unique holiness.
The Arizal could not fathom the secret of the lechem hapanim because it is the depth of the Jewish soul, which is deeper than any mitzvah.
Revealing the secrets of the Torah is revealing the hidden secret of every Jew, so Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai after the second Churban did what Yechezkel's Merkavah did after the first.
Lag BaOmer and Purim fall on the same weekday because both are for those who stumbled, the tribe of Dan whom the clouds did not protect and Amalek attacked.

Following Rav Tzadok, the Rav contrasts the mikveh, where a person exerts himself and goes down, with water sprinkled from above while he does nothing; Sefirah is the second kind, since the Yidden only count and the purity comes down from Hashem.
When Klal Yisrael reaches Hod shebeHod, Hashem is already at Tiferes shebeTiferes coming toward them, as a chassan goes out of the chuppah to meet his kallah; this is the special love of Lag Baomer.

The poor man receives grain that falls to the ground and grain that is forgotten because he himself is down on the ground and forgotten; in the same way, every kind of grain, and even the bread a Jew buys, has a connection to a particular soul.
The Rav reads 'vehenif es ha'Omer' as Hashem's command to the kohen, the tzaddik, to pick up the fallen Yidden, and ties it by gematria to 'Sukkas David hanofeles'.
The two loaves of Shavuos are chametz, unlike every other mincha, because by then the chametz itself has gone through the lifting of the Omer and all the Yidden are holy.
Tisha B'Av is a moed because it belongs to those who had the ability to be great but ruined themselves; they will be rebuilt, and it will become the greatest simcha.
The double measure of flour with the Omer, though a sheep normally takes one, reflects a double purification: the Yidden count, and Hashem counts.
The fourfold Torah of pshat, remez, drush and sod is mirrored in every Jew: what people see is only his pshat, while his sod, the trait that makes him dear to Hashem, stays hidden.
The Gemara counts the talmidim as 12,000 pairs to show where the flaw lay: in each pair the lesser chavrusa honored the greater, but the greater did not honor the lesser.
The dying stopped in the week of Hod because Hod, yielding, is exactly the middah that teaches a greater person to respect a lesser one.
The date of Pesach Sheini, which commemorates nothing from Yetzias Mitzrayim, has no explanation on purpose: it is a sod, like the hidden worth of the temei'im it was given to.
The calendar sign 'peleg', that Lag BaOmer falls on Purim's weekday, reveals that both days celebrate the hidden worth of the lowest Jews.
Unlike the Torah of other Tannaim and poskim, which speaks to those who can learn it, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's revelation of sod speaks to the simplest Jew, telling him he too carries a secret.
The final date of the Geulah is the greatest sod, since it comes even for complete reshaim by virtue of the sod each of them carries.
The Sefirah mourning ends on Lag BaOmer because hod shebehod is the Kodesh HaKodashim and Rashbi is its Kohen Gadol after the churban, and a Kohen Gadol is untouched by mourning.

Rashbi's revealing of the hidden Torah is the revealing of the hidden point in every Jew, since each soul corresponds to a letter of the Sefer Torah; this is the cure for the sin of Rabbi Akiva's students.
The students' failure was not a lack of false modesty, since one may truly know more than his chavrusa; what they missed is the unseen point in which the other is superior.

The makom ha'aron was not counted among the miracles of the Beis HaMikdash because it was permanent; like the different laws of the sea or of Heaven, the Kodesh HaKodashim simply has laws above time and space.
The four seasons in which sedras are combined are exactly the times connected to redemption and to the breach of achdus, including Sefirah, when Rabbi Akiva's students fell.
Lag BaOmer falls on Purim's day of the week because both are hod, days that bring out the hidden worth of every Jew even when he is accused.
Counting the 24 letters of Baruch Shem and then the letters of Shema, the 33rd letter is the first yud of Hashem's name, the point that contains the other letters: Lag BaOmer is that point.

The hierarchy of the Sefer Torah, from letter to word to column to parshah, mirrors Klal Yisrael from individual to family to shevet to the Avos, and Eretz Yisrael is divided the same way, with Yerushalayim as the shared root above the shevatim.
Tiferes is like a niggun: not every combination of notes is music, as a cat walking on a piano shows; the harmony that blends opposites creates something new.

Sefirah is counted from both sides: Klal Yisrael, the kallah, counts from Chesed down, while Hashem, the chassan going out toward her, counts from Malchus up, and on that count Lag BaOmer is Tiferes sheb'Tiferes.

The combined sedras at the edges of Nisan and Tishrei, in Sefirah and in the Three Weeks are a repair for sinas chinam, breaking the barriers between groups of Jews whose Shabbosos are otherwise separate.

The dispute over the most honored aliyah, shlishi or shishi, is an echo of the old strife between Yehuda and Yosef, and the Midrash of the Yam Suf, created on the third day, yielding to man, created on the sixth, shows that when Jews are in trouble seniority quarrels must give way.

A leap year needs no combined sedras because the extra month lets the lunar year catch up with the solar year, undoing the diminishing of the moon; the word 'haSheni' in Adar Sheni has the numerical value 365, matching the sun's days.
The eved nirtza has fallen so low that when Shemitah throws him a rope he does not grab it; only Yovel, the great return, takes him out, and Rashbi's mitzvah is this Yovel.
Bringing Jews back to Yerushalayim, in the Rambam's sign of Moshiach, is not a geographical matter but bringing them back to their roots and to serving Hashem.

The jealousy that killed Rabbi Akiva's students, began with the moon, and runs through Kayin, Yosef's brothers and the kings, is the same baseless hatred that destroyed the Beis HaMikdash, the place of unity; Moshiach and Rashbi repair it.

The Gemara tells of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza to teach that the last small act completes what generations accumulated: just as they gave the last tug to destruction, the last generation, like a child, will give the last tug to the building.

Through the At-Bash rule, Pesach does not tell us when Purim was; rather Purim looks forward to the coming Pesach, the Pesach of the future redemption, and Lag Ba'omer, which falls on Purim's weekday, likewise heralds Moshiach.

Yovel's two promises, return to one's holding and return to one's family, match nefesh and the higher levels: Pesach Sheni restores only property, while Lag Ba'omer restores the higher level of family.

The Rav reads the two parts of a fingernail as two kinds of distant Jews: the part still attached, painful to remove, is the sinner who still believes and comes to shul on Yom Kippur; the protruding part, cut off painlessly, is the heretic.
Cutting the nails before Shabbos stands for the Jew who refuses Shabbos's rescue, like one who does not catch the rope thrown to him; Shabbos can do nothing for him, but Yovel still brings him back.
Rus is said to have 'returned' to a land she had never been in, which shows that she was a Jewish soul snatched away by the Sitra Achra and born in the palace of the king of Moav.

The week of Hod is bracketed by two days of second chances: Pesach Sheni for those excluded from the Exodus, and Lag Ba'omer, Hod sheb'Hod, the lowest level, where holiness is strong enough to reach the very bottom.
There is no mourning by Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai for the same reason the Kohen Gadol does not mourn: one connected to the Holy of Holies, the place of complete unity, lacks nothing.
The Kosel and Meron are the two places where the entire spectrum of Jews, from the greatest tzaddik to the greatest sinner, still comes together, because Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is like the Mikdash.
Just as Shabbos kept Adam HaRishon in Gan Eden, Shabbos keeps Lag Ba'omer, which falls on Friday this year, from leaving, giving two days of Lag Ba'omer.
The Rav compares the descent of Hashem's attributes into human middos to water passing from invisible vapor to steam, water and ice: the same substance, more physical the further it comes down.
A mother clutching her baby on the stairs shows gevurah within chesed: her fear is aroused by her love.
According to the Rav, Yishmael's milah without a bris is an empty milah, which is why it earned him Eretz Yisroel only while the land was empty of Jews.
The sa'ir to Azazel carries Israel's sins to Esav because a Jew's inner will is always to do Hashem's will; the sin belongs to the yetzer hara, Esav's angel.
Yishmael, the klipah of yesod, always pursues Yosef, the tzaddik of yesod; it was Yishmaelim who brought Yosef down to Mitzrayim, the ervas ha'aretz.
The Rav reads the world's attention on Eretz Yisroel as a screen of a heavenly din Torah, whose real front is a bochur in the street who turns his eyes away.

The Rav defines serving Hashem with chesed as a love so strong it makes no calculations, like the Rambam's lovesick person who pays no attention to anything else, and he sees this in the Jews following Hashem into a barren desert.

Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Rav explains that the Torah calls a forbidden union 'chesed' because it is the very middah of chesed, created for loving Hashem, Torah and Jews, turned toward what is forbidden.

Netzach and hod are the two legs: one stands by prevailing and by yielding, as animals in the jungle either fight or give way; in holiness this means defeating false views and conceding to the truth, while winning in learning only to show off is impure.
Customs that once expressed holy love for the Rebbe, such as pushing toward him or grabbing shirayim, become bad middos when people are no longer on that level, and that is why Rebbes abolished them.

The Pirkei Avos of each week matches that week's sefirah: the first chapter, with 'from the mouth of the Gevurah', in the week of gevurah, and the second, opening with tiferes, in the week of tiferes.

A mikveh purifies like a sefer Torah written according to halachah: its waters are bound with holy names, so the higher the names, the higher the mikveh, and on Shavuos morning different names enter it.
The Exodus on the first night was a gift that brought the Jews to the level of the Avos; the forty-nine days are the work of earning that same level by oneself.
Over nearly two thousand years of galus, each generation or era passes through one of the forty-nine desert journeys, until the redemption and the entry into Eretz Yisrael.
Going back to repeat the whole line of Ana B'koach after each week mirrors the seven journeys the Jews went back in the desert, turning forty-two into forty-nine.

The Omer of barley, animal food, is a sotah's offering testing the Jews' purity; reaching Shavuos with the wheat loaves, human food, shows they were found pure, and the milui of Hashem's Name beside the brachah equals adam.
The last day of the count, malchus shebemalchus, matches the last daf of Sotah, which speaks of ikvesa d'meshicha, the lowest level of galus right before the redemption.
Prices rising even when supply is plentiful defy the law of supply and demand, and the Rav reads this as the Baraisa's sign that wine will be dear though the vine gives its fruit.

The rule of making the brachah over the more important food is not about valuing quality for its own sake, but because the more important food awakens a stronger feeling of thanks, which is the point of a brachah.

The advantage of a whole loaf is of a different kind: not gratitude but shleimus, on which Hashem's Name rests, as learned from the kohen and korban with a blemish; this is why Rabbi Yochanan uses a different wording from Rav Huna.

Jews do not gain their bond to Olam Haba, Torah and Eretz Yisrael through mitzvos; the reverse is true: because they are bound to them, they were given mitzvos. This is why the Torah opens with Bereishis rather than the first mitzvah.

Just as a Jew and a non-Jew, and Shabbos and the weekdays, are different in kind, Eretz Yisrael is the 'Jewish land' whose inner essence is Torah and Shabbos; therefore it too keeps Shabbos, and its Yovel parallels Yom Kippur, the Shabbos of Shabbos.

The seven nations of Canaan are the seven middos; conquering the land means refining one's own middos during the seven weeks of Sefirah, until even the weekdays become 'Jewish' and everything is drawn into Shabbos.
The shedim were left without bodies not for lack of time but because they were created lacking shleimus, so that they could have no connection to Shabbos, which is wholeness.
Shavuos is the one festival whose day is fixed by every Jew's counting rather than by Beis Din, which shows that the giving of the Torah belongs to each Jew.
Even a Jew who seems simple holds the Torah within him, and it can come out in his child as a great talmid chacham.
Jews differ only on the surface; beneath it every Jew has the same power for Torah.

Netzach and hod are the two legs on which a person stands: netzach survives by resisting, hod survives like grass that bends before the storm while cedars break; for a Jew, the ability to submit is itself beauty.

The Holy of Holies, Yom Kippur and the Kohen Gadol are one point in place, time and soul; so Aharon is the 'soul-Beis Hamikdash', and his death in Av, the month of hod, foreshadowed the churban in the same month.

The minyan is learned specifically from the meraglim to show that ten Jews, even reshaim, reveal the inner point where none is wicked, which nine tzaddikim cannot do; there is no need to emend the Gemara.

Since Hashem makes no duplicates, each Jew has a purpose no one else can fulfill, and in that point the worst Jew is greater than the greatest tzaddik; this is what Rabbi Akiva's students failed to see.

Chazal derive mourning from a festival because its root is joy: mourning belongs only to the body, and Tisha B'Av always falls on the weekday of Pesach, showing that Jewish mourning is rooted in redemption.

After the churban Hashem sent Rashbi's soul to fill the place of the Beis Hamikdash; the inner Torah was revealed to him precisely while he was hidden in the cave, as the inner place is never revealed.
'Ohr' equals 'raz': the inner point is a secret even from oneself, yet it gives light, and this is why Lag BaOmer is marked with so much fire and light.

The lowest point of the sefirah tikkun, hod sheb'hod, is exactly where the highest light, that of Moshe, Moshiach and Rashbi, shines, just as the Torah's last parsha, tied to the lowest souls, is joined to Bereishis.
Because the fiftieth day is above time, Moshe's added day before Matan Torah is not really another day: one cannot count it on a calendar of torn-off pages.
Aharon is himself 'kodesh kodashim': as hod and the Beis Hamikdash is hod, he is the Beis Hamikdash in the soul, which is why he alone may enter the Holy of Holies.
Aveilus is only relative to this world; the Kodesh haKodashim is the 'embassy' of the World to Come, so the Kohen Gadol, and Rashbi's place in Meron, stand outside mourning.

In pshat the large beis of Bereishis outranks the lamed of 'l'einei kol Yisrael', but in sod the last is bound to the first and the lamed has a virtue even the beis lacks; so every Jew, however small, is indispensable.
The 'pnei Elokim' Jews long to see is the innermost part of the name Elokim, which is pure mercy; only its outer side is judgment.
Lag Baomer always falls on the weekday of Purim, and both are days for the lowly whose hidden worth an outsider like Amalek cannot see.

Chanoch, who withdrew and became an angel but neglected his generation, embodies 'Hashem'; Avraham, who went down to the lowest people, embodies 'Elokeichem'; 'kedoshim tihyu' asks for holiness that does not contradict closeness to people.
Nissan is the birth of creation and Tishrei its bar mitzvah; Rabbi Eliezer, a man of din, holds the world was created in Tishrei, and Rabbi Yehoshua, of Beis Hillel's chesed, in Nissan.
The first se'ir of Rosh Chodesh was burned not as a failure but as the best sign: on the day of the Mishkan the moon was whole, so the atonement for its lessening was not needed.

Nadav and Avihu entered after drinking wine because they already felt the time of Eliyahu, when the Gemara says one will be able to make wine a fixed meal and wine will no longer harm; it was a sign of their greatness.

Yayin (70) is the Name of Hashem (26) plus dam (44): a little wine, used for kedushah, is the Name, while too much leaves only blood; this is why Kiddush begins 'Yom hashishi vayechulu', whose initials spell the Name.
Sefirah and Elul-Tishrei each last fifty-one days, and the thirtieth day of each, Pesach Sheni and Rosh Hashanah, is a day of tikkun.
The three teshuvah seasons follow nature: Nissan, when roots sprout, repairs the middos; Tishrei, the harvest, repairs deeds; Shovavim is a laundry season to remove the stains left after teshuvah.
The Seder night's leap out of the 49 gates was an unearned gift that faded; the counting of sefirah is the work of earning the same level oneself, one gate a day.
Every generation of galus is one of the 49 journeys of the desert, so the whole exile is one long sefirah leading to the geulah.

The omer offering is of barley, animal food, like the sotah's offering, because during sefirah the Jews stand under suspicion like a sotah; on Shavuos, cleared, they bring loaves of wheat, human food.
The daf of Sotah learned on erev Shavuos, the day of malchus shebemalchus, is exactly the mishnah of the footsteps of Moshiach, the lowest point of galus.
The high prices of the footsteps of Moshiach are notable because they defy the law of supply and demand: the vine gives its fruit, yet wine is expensive.
Minus is worse than idolatry: an idolater who believed in a false god still held himself back, but one who believes in nothing has no one to restrain him.

The Rav applies the Ohr HaChaim's parable of flies on an emptied barrel of honey to the yoledes: her tumah is not a defect but the residue of the great holiness of carrying a child who learned Torah with an angel.

Because a bris borrows a few moments of the days of Moshiach, when Eliyahu, who never ate from the Etz HaDaas, is present, the tumah that came from the sin of Adam is cut short; this is why the yoledes of a boy is tamei for less time.
The verse of milah on the eighth day interrupts the laws of the yoledes to answer the question the reader is about to ask, why a boy brings less tumah than a girl.
Shavuos is both the fiftieth day and the first day of the eighth week, like the eighth day on which a tamei person immerses; the day of Shavuos is itself the mikveh.
The days of Sefirah are a davar shebeminyan: like counted, important items that are never nullified even in a thousand, the counted days are too precious to be lost.
Rabbi Akiva's students died specifically between Pesach and Shavuos because in these weeks of preparing for Matan Torah, lacking midos is judged more strictly than during the rest of the year.
Since a person is where his thoughts are, one who speaks lashon hara is not allowed to direct his Shemoneh Esrei toward Yerushalayim, and so is exiled from Yerushalayim even today.
The Aron that Shlomo hid beneath the Kodesh HaKodashim corresponds to the ahavah mesuteres, the concealed love of Hashem hidden in every Jew's heart, which churban never reaches.
The vavim, the only part of the Mishkan outside the camp, were made from the extra half-shekels, which presumably came from the Jews who had fallen outside the camp; that is why Moshe forgot them.
Rabbi Akiva's name contains the word akev, the heel: his soul reaches down to the lowest Jews, and so it was he who reminded Moshe of the forgotten ones.
The Torah shares the fate of the Jews: just as they are scattered in galus, its halachos are scattered, with laws of Shabbos found in Menachos and the reverse.
Yishmael's strength is the bow, the middah of yesod he holds through milah; Lag Ba'omer, completing hod shebehod, is when Klal Yisrael seizes that bow from him.

The 70 tikkunim of the Tikkunei Zohar, each an explanation of the word Bereishis, repair the seventy faces of Klal Yisrael, connecting the end to the beginning; "vayehi roveh kashes" equals "shivim tikkunim" in gematria.
Eliyahu's promise that the Jews will leave exile through the Zohar applies to all the sefarim built on it, especially chassidus, because the Ba'al Shem Tov was the soul of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai.

Following the Ramchal, the 'shevi', the captive that Moshe brought down from on high with great difficulty, is the soul of Rabbi Shimon, and the same letters recur in the names of the Arizal and the Ba'al Shem Tov, souls that reveal the secrets of the Torah.
'Rotzeh ani', the inner will of a Jew that the Rambam says is real even when it comes out under compulsion, equals Yom Kippur in gematria, and Yom Kippur reveals it in every Jew.

Purim reveals the inner core of a Jew, which is why the simplest Jews rejoice on Purim more than elevated ones, and Rabbi Shimon himself revealed this when he taught that the Jews in Haman's time sinned only outwardly.

Counting the omer and every other remembrance of the Beis Hamikdash is a way of seeking Zion that arouses a seeking of Zion above, and Lag Ba'omer, which comes from the Holy of Holies, the summit of Zion, is a whole day of it.
Like Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, the Jews in Eretz Yisrael have become so accustomed to miracles that they no longer notice them.
Gevurah, though itself judgment, is close to binah, with only chesed between them; hod is far removed, the lowest of the middos of judgment, and so the hardest to sweeten.
The letters of hod reversed spell the impurity of blood that Eichah ascribes to Yerushalayim: the overturned hod is the red of judgment.
Lag Ba'Omer is the start of the last third of sefirah, like the dawn watch of the night, and from it the count already connects to the fiftieth day.
The custom of dairy on Shavuos expresses the completion of sefirah's work: the blood of din has been whitened into milk, the chesed that began flowing on Lag Ba'Omer.

Av, the fifth month, mirrors the fifth middah: the Beis Hamikdash fell then, and the fifth of Av, hod shebehod of Av, is the passing of the Arizal, a gilgul of Rabbi Shimon, just as Lag Ba'Omer is hod shebehod of sefirah.
The Arizal's Torah stayed in the hidden realm, with no halachos from him, while Rabbi Shimon's teachings came down also into the Mishnah and braisos, the world of pshat.
Rabbi Shimon is the soul of 'al tishkechi kol gemulav', the passuk from which the Gemara learns that milk was placed at the seat of binah, so he is the one who sweetens.
The Rema is the revealed side of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, which is why the Rema's yahrzeit falls on Rabbi Shimon's day.
Rabbi Shimon's way was the dove, which finds the hidden good even in the tochacha; the Rema's way, as the revealed Torah, was the raven, which exposes what is not in order.
Because Rabbi Shimon expounded the secret of each letter, and each letter is a Jew, he expounded the hidden tzaddik in every Jew, even in the lowliest.

The 'lightest of the light', the souls found in the tochacha, also carry a hidden secret; the passuk there that is the fiftieth mention of the Exodus holds the fiftieth gate and the secret of the geulah.
The Rav reads 'mipi zaro' in Rabbi Shimon's proof as a hint to his own name, Bar Yochai, through whom the Torah will not be forgotten.
The higher a light is, the lower it reaches; therefore Rabbi Shimon's joy grows as the generations go down, and later generations feel more light on Lag BaOmer than earlier ones did.
The breaking of the vessels came from the receivers' refusal to submit to the giver, the claim "I will rule", like a cup that wants to stand higher than the pitcher and so receives nothing.

The eighth king of Edom, who has no "and he died" and whose wife is named, stands for a receiver that receives from the giver without breaking; the Rav brings that "in this year of Yovel" equals the wife's name in gematria.
A table is called shulchan because the food on it was sent (shalach) by Hashem to the person, as a mission to repair the sparks in it.
Unlike other Yamim Tovim, Lag BaOmer grows greater as night falls, because this Yom Tov comes down to the person rather than requiring him to rise to it.
The companions held hands in a closed circle like an electric circuit; talking or letting go in the middle of a dance breaks that circuit.
Rabbi Shimon is the soul that is Shabbos, and his view that all Jews are princes, all equal, will become the halacha when Moshiach comes.
Yovel is the fiftieth gate, where all Jewish souls merge into one soul, and this is the inner meaning of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, whose day gathers all Jews together.

The Gemara says Osniel ben Kenaz restored forgotten halachos because he conquered the matching part of the land; the Ba'al Shem Tov reads it the other way: learning the halachos is what conquers the land.
The hair of the first three years parallels the three years of orlah, and the fourth year's 'kodesh hilulim' is the gematria of Har Esav, so the upsherin stands against Esav.
The sons of Keturah have milah but no priah because their bodies come from the three impure kelipos and not from kelipas nogah, which priah addresses.
Lag BaOmer is the great fall of Esav, the 'head' struck in the passuk, and from it the attribute of chessed begins to lead toward the fiftieth day.

Yaakov could complete only the 24 letters of Baruch Shem because the Shechinah had no Mishkan yet; the 25 letters of the verse calling Moshe from the Ohel Moed show that the 25-letter unity became possible only once the Mishkan stood.

The order of saying Baruch Shem after Shema follows importance, but the order of tikkun was Yaakov's 24 first; counted that way, the 33rd letter falls on the first yud of Hashem's name, which is why Lag Baomer reveals the point of every Jew.

The four parts of Torah, pshat, remez, drush and sod, correspond to ascending worlds: Yaakov died only in the world of pshat, while in drush and above he lives, and so Rabbi Shimon, who revealed sod, did not die in that realm.
Both Yaakov and Rabbi Shimon passed away with the word 'chaim': Yaakov's last words ended with 'bnei Ches', and Rabbi Shimon died in the middle of saying 'chaim'.

Rabbi Akiva's students were surely respectful of a greater man; their failing was that the greater one did not honor the lesser, not recognizing the hidden sod in the other that makes him irreplaceable, like a letter without which a Sefer Torah is invalid.
The Rav reads the golden dinars of the valley as Rashbi's own Torah secrets, which lay spread over Meron and took material form only because the students showed interest in wealth.
Silver and gold are, spiritually, love and fear; only the constrictions of this world turn them into metal, so the material object is a lowered form of a spiritual level.
Today halacha follows Beis Hillel because this is a Torah of silver, of love; when Moshiach comes there will be a Torah of gold, of the attribute of judgment.

Because the gold was Torah already present in Meron rather than a gift from heaven, its vanishing needed no miracle, which answers why the Midrash speaks of a greater miracle only for Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta.
The halacha does not follow Rabbi Shimon only because he was not grasped; in the future, when the world is full of knowledge of Hashem, it will.
A Jew who does not take his heavenly bounty materially keeps it as spiritual wealth: the joy of a blatt Gemara and the warmth of shalosh seudos.
The Rav links the peace among animals in the days of Moshiach to friendship among Jewish children: when the children are friends, the animals too become friends of the Jews.
Lag BaOmer marks the repair of the fault for which Rabbi Akiva's students died: through Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, friendship returned among the students and to the world.
The bow and arrow the children shoot on Lag BaOmer are Torah and tefillah, the same weapons with which Yaakov Avinu overcame his enemies, since Onkelos renders his sword and bow as his prayers.
The Rav describes the enemies of the Jews as the tigers and wolves of the prophecy, who want to swallow them, and holds that they cannot harm the Jews because Jewish children learn Torah.
Iyar's combination keeps the first half of the Name in the order of chesed but reverses the second half, hei before vav, so the month carries some din alongside the straight combination of Nisan.
Because Torah is G-dliness itself, one who understands a piece of Gemara understands Hashem; this is the inner meaning of 'haskel veyado'a osi', which makes Iyar's combination a call to Torah.
Rav Chaim Vital merited to grasp the Arizal's deep Torah after the Arizal had him drink from Miriam's well in the Kinneret, which shows that the well, given in Iyar, brings Torah.
The days of Sefirah leave a greater mark than Tishrei; Tishrei is judgment with the attribute of din, so one fasts and says selichos, while Nisan through Sivan are judgment with chesed.
The three Shabbos meals match the three tefillos of the Avos, and melaveh malkah, the meal of Dovid, matches a fourth tefillah of tzaddikim, tikkun chatzos.
Yeshayahu, speaking of the future, mentions Rosh Chodesh even before Shabbos, because when Moshiach comes Rosh Chodesh will be like Shabbos and even more.

The Baal HaTurim's 'zekunim' leaves out Taharos not because Yaakov withheld it but because Yosef, the ro'eh corresponding to Seder Taharos, already knew it by himself; and that is why Yaakov loved him more, since he had less to teach him.
Yosef was not one of the twelve shevatim but one of the seven ro'im, which is why his sons took his place among the shevatim and why the brothers misread his elevated conduct as arrogance.

The future split of the sea into seven streams instead of twelve paths marks the elevation of the shevatim from separate branches to the level of the seven ro'im, a level touched already on Shabbos, when the twelve weekday requests give way to one brachah.

Because the first contains everything, Avraham, 'ba bayamim', comes with all seven days and knew the whole Torah by instinct, while each later av knew by himself only the order of Mishnah of his own day.

Taharah gives taste and fragrance: Yaakov recognized from the holy fragrance of the produce that came from impure Mitzrayim that Yosef, the embodiment of Seder Taharos, was handling it, which joins Rashi's and Targum Yonasan's readings into one.

Mishkan Shiloh, Yosef's sanctuary, had a quality Yerushalayim lacked: its holiness reached as far as it could be seen, a merit of Yosef's holy eyes; so Elul is Shiloh and the Ten Days are Yerushalayim.
Elul relates to Rosh Hashanah as Friday to Shabbos and as taharah to kedusha: without the purity of Elul one cannot reach 'HaMelech HaKadosh' of Rosh Hashanah.

The three places in the Torah that promise Moshiach correspond to the Rambam's three simanim: the war in Balak, the ingathering in Nitzavim, and strengthening the whole Torah in the mitzvah of the additional cities of refuge.

Since every Jew is rooted in one mitzvah, the Rav proposes that Moshiach's mitzvah is ir miklat: it is the one mitzvah all generations together have not yet fulfilled, so by adding the three cities he becomes the one who completes the Torah.

Kriyas Shema is the ir miklat within the Torah: its six opening words and the 42 words of 'V'ahavta' match the six cities and the 42 Levite cities, 48 in all, because acceptance of Malchus Shamayim is the refuge from the yetzer hara.
By gematria, 'v'yasafta lecha od shalosh' and 'az yavdil Moshe shalosh arim' both equal 'som tasim alecha melech', tying the cities of refuge to the mitzvah of appointing a king, Moshe and Moshiach.

The Satan does go first to Betzer, but senses Moshiach there, since Betzer in ribua gematria equals David ben Yishai, so he reasons that Bozrah is Betzer's feminine counterpart, because in tumah the feminine dominates.
Malchus is not native to Yisrael but imported from Moav, through Rus to Yisrael and through Bozrah to Edom, so the Satan flees from the malchus of kedushah to its counterpart in tumah.

The pesukim of the sedras read in this season match the stages of teshuvah: Vayelech 30, Nitzavim 40, Haazinu 52, together 122, the days to the end of Chanukah, while Ki Savo's 122 refer to last year.

Because shanah means repetition, the year is like a turning rotary file of days: when Rosh Hashanah comes around, what happened on that day, the creation of Adam with the breath of life, actually happens again.
The shofar answers the 'vayipach': Hashem blew His breath into us, and on the day that breath is renewed we blow it back to Him in His service.

The word 'Bereishis', the hidden tenth utterance that does not say 'vayomer', corresponds to the innermost point of the Jew, above speech and intellect, where no Jew wants to sin; this is the root of Yom Kippur's atonement, the tenth day.
The makri does not call out the first tekiah because at that level words have not yet been created; only after it does speech begin.
The ten pesukim each of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofaros are the ten utterances by which man re-creates the world, and the hundred sounds are ten times ten.
From the burning of the Beis HaMikdash on the tenth of Av until Rosh Hashanah is fifty days, so Rosh Hashanah is a fiftieth day of return like Shavuos and the Yovel, marked by the shofar.
Judgment is not the essence of Rosh Hashanah but a byproduct of the coronation: because Hashem is re-creating His world, He decides who belongs in it.
The word shanah, year, means repetition: each year the creation is repeated, with each of the ten days of teshuvah creating another part of the world, parallel to the ten utterances.
Since every new year is a higher world, a person who stays as he was last year fails, even if he got a good mark then; he must be promoted with the world.
Although earlier generations had greater souls, the innermost chamber of the heart, which longs for Hashem, grows better in each generation.
As there is a Kodesh HaKodashim in space, there is one in time, Yom Kippur, and one in every Jew's heart, the point that wants only Hashem's will.
Keeping Shabbos Shuvah, as testimony to creation, makes a Jew a partner in Hashem's creation of the new year.
The shofar is the regular advocate on Rosh Hashanah, and when it is silent on Shabbos, Shabbos replaces it as an even better advocate, since she is the King's own daughter.
Shabbos is called the Jew's cousin, since both come from the same heavenly source and on Shabbos it becomes part of the Jewish soul as the neshamah yeseirah.
Chillul Shabbos is pictured as the servant abusing the princess: the very one who must plead for the Jews could instead bring out their guilt unless they first make peace with her.
Because Hashem created the world through speech in the six days and rested on Shabbos, a Jew's resting on Shabbos must include speech that is unlike weekday speech.
The measure of keeping Shabbos is whether Shabbos itself derives pleasure from the way it is kept; Shabbos then reciprocates with a pleasure no worldly delight can match.
Hashem's love for Noach lay in saving him even after the plan of a perfected world from the teiva had failed through the sins in the teiva, a love rooted in the future of Avraham and Klal Yisrael.
Noach's drinking reflected his mistaken belief that the world after the flood was already perfected, when it was not.

The shofar parallels the utterance of Bereishis, which has no stated speech because it precedes speech, and parallels the breath Hashem blew into Adam on Rosh Hashanah; so the shofar's wordless sound creates a world above sin and above physicality.
The Klausenberger Rebbe valued the leining of Sarah's demand to expel Yishmael above the shofar, as a way to arouse in Heaven that Yishmael should have no share in Eretz Yisrael.
The second day's reading continues the first: the Akeidah is the culmination of Yitzchak's victory over Yishmael, which is why Yishmael is called an enemy while Eisav is only a hater.
Rejoicing in the King's coronation, even on one's own day of judgment, is itself the merit that transforms the verdict.

The Rav reads the Gemara's statement that the Mikdash is 'higher' than all lands not physically but as the top of the globe, the point where Hashem first touched creation and from which the whole world grew.

He connects Har, mountain, with herayon, conception, and hirhur, thought, with 'a mountain on top of a mountain', so that Rosh Hashanah is the conception of the year and Yom Kippur the thought that precedes even that.

He finds the same pattern of a forty-day formation in soul and time: the forty days of an embryo's formation, and the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur, which set the destiny of the whole year.

Origins are elusive because they begin in thought; this is why Shmuel did not recognize David, why David and Shmuel first erred about the Mikdash's site, and why the Levi'im erred about Rosh Hashanah.

The Sanhedrin's authority depends on sitting in the place of the Mikdash because that place is the origin of Torah, and Torah is the blueprint of the world; so Yerushalayim, the center of the world, should appear in the middle of the Torah.
The ten pesukim of each of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofros correspond to the ten utterances of creation, so that saying them with the shofar is an act of recreating the world and oneself.
The Ba'alei Mussar read Hashem's availability in the ten days through Rav standing at the butcher's door: the same nearness that is a gift becomes grounds for a greater punishment when it is ignored.
Carrying the Sefer Torah around the shul on Yom Kippur night enacts the same idea: the Torah comes to us, so that each Jew can kiss it and ask its forgiveness.
Yom Kippur is itself the 'Shabbos of Shabbosos', into which all the Shabbosos of the year flow; when it falls on Shabbos, each day fortifies the other.
In the Arvei Nachal's mashal, Shabbos and the Torah are the king's daughter and son who defend Klal Yisrael, and the advice is to fall at their feet and ask their forgiveness.
Since Hashem created the world with speech and rested on the seventh day, the rest of Shabbos includes rest from ordinary speech.
A mikveh can take different forms: forty se'ah of water, a day in time, and on Yom Kippur Hashem Himself is the mikveh.

Through the Chiddushei HaRim, the Rav reads 'Magen Avraham' as Hashem shielding the hidden point of Avraham Avinu in every Jew, like a pilot light that can set the whole person aflame with love and fear of Hashem.

The forty lashes of the Torah correspond to the forty days of forming a person, and only thirty-nine are given because the fortieth point never sinned; the same count explains Adam's thirty-nine curses and the thirty-nine melachos of Shabbos.
Yom Kippur is the fortieth day of teshuvah, corresponding to that fortieth point, and so on it a Jew reaches the Holy of Holies in his own heart where no Satan or angel enters.
On Yom Kippur, unlike any other tefillah, even Rosh Hashanah, Hashem speaks back to the Jew in the tefillos, saying He erases his sins and calls him to return.
The Rav reads the Ba'al HaTanya's statement that we cannot bow today as meaning that real bowing, surrender of one's existence, can only be done in the place of Malchus; elsewhere it would be false.

Following the Sefer Yetzirah's parallel of place, time and soul, the Kodesh HaKodashim in place corresponds to Yom Kippur in time and to the Kohen Gadol in soul, and the ten days of teshuvah are the Beis HaMikdash in time.
There is no mitzvah to go to Yerushalayim on Yom Kippur, the holiest day, because on these days one need not come to the place of Malchus: Malchus comes to us.
The custom that the chazzan of Shacharis calls out HaMelech from his place before walking to the amud shows that the King comes to us wherever we are.
The dog is despised because it is dependent on a substitute master and happy with him; true freedom is to be a servant of Hashem alone.

The Rav reads the thirty-nine lashes through the Rambam's rule of compelled consent: the beatings only suppress the body, and the Rabbanan, who see into the depth of a Jew, know that his innermost fortieth level never consented to the sin.
He maps the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul onto the forty days of a child's formation, so that the year is formed in these days and Yom Kippur is its fortieth stage.
The thirty-nine lashes on Erev Yom Kippur match the thirty-nine days before it; the fortieth day, Yom Kippur itself, needs no lash because then the true will comes out.
Each of the forty days adds a se'ah, so Yom Kippur completes the mikveh of Klal Yisrael; an unresolved quarrel is then a chatzitzah that keeps the mikveh from working.
The 'proof' the tailor brought was the price itself: no one pays far beyond worth unless out of love, and since Hashem returns the love shown to Him, the overpayment proves forgiveness.

The Rav reads the Rambam's coerced consent as the body being pushed aside so that the soul, which always wants Hashem's will, can speak, and identifies this inner will with the Yechida that Yom Kippur reveals.

From the Ohr HaChaim on Korach the Rav derives that a sinner's blemish climbs up through his ancestry but stops before Yaakov Avinu, the trunk of the tree, so no Jew can fall low enough to damage that point in himself.

The Rav links the missing fortieth lash to the first day of a person's formation, when he was in direct contact with his Creator, and finds the same thirty-nine-not-forty pattern in Adam's curses and the melachos of Shabbos.
He suggests that the image of his father that Yosef saw was the point of Yaakov Avinu within himself, the same point a Jew is meant to meet on Yom Kippur.

The Rav explains that lashes are received on Erev Yom Kippur, the thirty-ninth day of the forty from Rosh Chodesh Elul, and that this is why the Torah's lashes stop at thirty-nine: the fortieth day is Yom Kippur, where no sin reaches.
He describes the forty days of Elul as pouring one se'ah of teshuvah a day into the mikveh of Yom Kippur, so that on Yom Kippur the mikveh is complete.

The Rav explains that the Tzedukim's logic, that a king's meal is prepared outside, is correct for a king, but on Yom Kippur Hashem relates to Yisrael as husband to wife, and alone together the wife may prepare the food in his presence.

He ties the dispute to Torah sheba'al peh: the Chachmei Yisrael are the mistress of the house who run its affairs, and the Tzedukim, who denied this, rejected the whole concept of Yisrael as Hashem's beloved.
He explains that the Chachamim gave no reply in the Yerushalmi because this is not a single point that one argument can settle; it is an entire outlook, and one who rejects it cannot be answered.
Only in the Shemoneh Esrei of Yom Kippur does Hashem speak to us, in the words 'shuvah eilai ki ge'alticha', showing that the relationship of chassan and kallah belongs to Yom Kippur.
Since smell was the one sense not damaged by the sin of the Eitz HaDa'as, the ketores and Shir HaShirim, both built on fragrance, express a love that never suffers any blemish.
The Tzeduki Kohen Gadol was punished with worms coming out of his nose, the organ of smell, because he denied the sense of smell and the level of Shir HaShirim.
Before the war, the failure to know or think seriously about what the coming year held was itself part of the decree of concealment.

At the end of the year the old year's merits are spent and the new year's have not begun, so the world stands on Hashem's kindness alone until the tefillos and shofar create it anew; this is why the night of Rosh Hashana is a time of fearsome judgment.

A thing's right to exist after Rosh Hashana depends on its being part of Hashem's kingship; even a stone has a life-force suited to it, and when the judgment withdraws that life-force the thing breaks.
Each of the 365 days corresponds to one of the 365 negative mitzvos, so that Tisha B'Av corresponds to the prohibition of gid hanasheh, the portion of Esav, and on it Jews do not eat.

Shema, the tenth pasuk of Malchuyos, lacks the word melech for the same reason that Bereishis, the first of the ten maamaros, lacks 'vayomer': it is the root from which the rest begins, the acceptance through which Hashem becomes King.
Rosh Hashana is to the year what the morning Shema is to the day, and Elul is to Rosh Hashana what the long preparation of Shacharis is to Shema.

Because there is no king without a people, a person who will not accept Hashem's kingship on Rosh Hashana has, in the Rav's words, no right to exist in the King's land, like a man who refuses allegiance to the king of a country.

The joy of Rosh Hashana is not in spite of the judgment but is the defense in it: like the prisoner who forgot his own trial for the king's joy, a Jew who rejoices in Hashem's kingship is granted a good year.
Which of the shofar's two reasons applies to a person depends on his Elul: after teshuvah he hears praise of the King; without it the shofar makes him tremble.
The name Elishama, nasi of Ephraim whose month is Tishrei, has the letters of Yishmael rearranged, showing that Tishrei is the time of the battle against Yishmael.
Zion is the seventh barren one, so Rosh Hashana, the time of remembering the barren, is also a time to pray for Zion to be remembered with her children's return.
Spiritual barrenness also counts: one whose learning and tefillah bear no fruit can be remembered on Rosh Hashana.
The Rav links the Midrash of the maiden who seized an angel's wings to Elul: the mazal of Elul was itself born of an act of grabbing, so that is the influence flowing down in this month.
The moment of a person's passing is the culmination of his whole life; therefore Binyamin, who came out together with Rachel's soul, is the quintessence of his mother.
Rachel gave away what was hers; Binyamin, her essence, has the merit to grab back what Esav wants to keep for himself.
Esav's share in the months is only an outer hold, since the whole creation belongs to Yisrael; what Yaakov and Binyamin grab is what is truly theirs.
Binyamin grabbed at both ends: the end of Av at Tu B'Av and the start of Teves at Chanukah.
One need not be a Lubavitcher to be on shlichus: every Jew is a shaliach of the Ribono shel Olam, sent into a world full of impurity to stay holy there.
Saying Tikunei Zohar in Elul is not only learning: it is a tikun of souls that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai performs for the Jewish people in these days.
Because all Jews are bound to one another, the few who say Tikunei Zohar help the whole people.
The rectification of these days is described as returning to Bereishis, the word on which the Tikunei Zohar is built, and binding oneself to the Ribono shel Olam.
The Rav treats the whole of Parshas Ki Seitzei, not only isolated mitzvos in it, as one parsha of tikkunei neshamos that fits the season of Elul.
A simple lechaim at a tzaddik's hilulah is, in his words, a tikkun for the tzaddik's soul.
Because each Shabbos is drawn from the parsha of its week, the character of the parsha becomes the character of the Shabbos.

The Rav reads the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur as the formation of the year, parallel to the forty days in which the Gemara says one may still pray about a fetus; with the Ba'al HaTurim he reads a 'male' year as one of brachah.
The count of pesukim in each parshah, recorded by the Masorah, is itself part of the Torah and carries meaning that can be darshened.

The parshiyos read in the season of teshuvah are layered like its windows of judgment: forty pesukim in Nitzavim for the beinonim's forty days, thirty more for the tzaddikim, fifty-two through Haazinu, and 122 in all for those who have until Zos Chanukah.
The Torah gives two signs of 122: Ki Savo looks back at last year's unused 122 days as an accusing finger, while Nitzavim through Haazinu open the new 122 days.
Following the Chafetz Chaim, the Rav teaches that a disaster in a far place like the Mississippi, or a storm in New York, is a messenger of Hashem meant to awaken the Jews.
Bringing the Maharal, the Rav says that where there is no Beis HaMikdash, the place where Jews sit and learn halacha is the Beis HaMikdash.
The Rav reads the world's frightening events as the shofar of Elul: in a time of great hester panim Hashem does not blow it openly but in another way, through what happens in the world.
He describes the Torah as having returned to Eretz Yisroel after it left with the churban; it was thought to have settled in America, but there it only made a stop.

According to the Rav one need not search the sefarim for hints about the coming year: the hints of Moshiach's coming can be seen in the newspaper, in what is happening in the world and in Eretz Yisroel.
He explains Rachel's jealousy of her sister as a kosher jealousy: one does not begrudge the other at all, and only wants to be like him too.
The Rav joins the Zohar's statement that Yaakov grabbed Elul with the Midrash that Elul's mazal, Besulah, was itself a maiden who grabbed an angel's wings, so the month's very nature is grabbing.
He reverses the usual fear: rather than the sitra achra grabbing a piece of a person, the person must grab a piece from the sitra achra for himself.

Because the moment of passing holds a whole life, and Rochel's soul left with Binyamin's birth, Binyamin carries his mother's essence of giving away her own, and that is what gives him the power to grab back.
Tu B'Av, when Binyamin's men grabbed wives at Shiloh, marks the point from which the season returns to Yaakov's portion, making it a day of grabbing.
Sitting at Rochel's grave on the last day of Av, at the edge of the grabbed month, is for the Rav the moment to resolve not to be grabbed by the yetzer hara.
The Ramban's reading of Haazinu as a testimony makes the parsha itself a proof of emunah: what has already come true guarantees what has not yet, which is why it is a segulah for emunah.
Because writing Haazinu means writing the whole Torah, and each Jew is one of the Torah's letters, Haazinu, a miniature of the Torah, contains every Jewish soul.
The place of the hint is itself the message: first letters are a Jew's root and last letters his end, which can never be erased; only the middle letters, a passing state, could carry Avner's erasure.
The Shabbos that contains the whole year reads the parsha that contains the whole Torah and every soul, so that all souls and all of the year can be repaired on it.

Like the Megillah, whose miracle is understood to begin from its first verse only once the king's sleepless night revealed it, the redemption the Arizal saw for 5736 may already have begun without being seen.
A person is like a switch: accepting Hashem's kingship on oneself is what turns on His kingship over the whole world.
In tefillah we speak to Hashem and in Torah He speaks to us; that is why only the middle brachah of Yom Kippur contains pesukim, for on Yom Kippur Hashem speaks to the Jew as a Father.

The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur are the 'formation' of the new year, like the forty days of an embryo's formation, during which prayer can still decide whether the year is a 'male' of blessing or a 'female' of curse.

Under the orlah of the heart, as under the orlah of a bris, lies the Divine Name; 'mi ya'aleh lanu hashamayma' begins with the letters of milah and ends with the letters of the Name, teaching that one ascends to heaven through milah, and in Elul Hashem Himself is the mohel.

The twenty-sixth day counted from Rosh Chodesh Elul matches the numerical value of the Divine Name, and 'umal Hashem' is the twenty-sixth verse of the sedra, while its fortieth and last verse, 'ki hu chayecha', corresponds to Yom Kippur, the fortieth day.

The mazal of Elul, the maiden, is the one who escaped a force far stronger than herself by taking the angel's own wings; likewise the yetzer hara is an angel, and a Jew escapes him by using his own fire and wings to fly to Hashem.

Shevet Dan, cast out of the Clouds of Glory measure for measure, were given the task of returning lost objects, because lost souls are the ones whose mission is to bring back what was lost; Elul, in the cycle of camps and books, is Dan's time.
The verse says the dispersed will be gathered 'from the end of the heavens', not of the earth: however far a Jew falls, a thread of heaven still goes with him, by which he can pull himself up.

Chana mentioned nursing rather than her other organs as a way of praying through gates that were still open, just as the Gemara prefers praying about hunger over plague, since granting sustenance includes granting life.
The Rav reads 'Let there be light' as the creation of liberty, so that each twenty-fifth of Elul is a renewal of the gift of freedom to the world.
He describes the whole world as a big prison: people think they are free, but whoever must obey his yetzer hara has no free choice.

Serving Hashem from the darkness of galus and chutz la'aretz, especially in the low generations before Moshiach, is an avodah that even the generation of Moshe Rabbeinu did not have, and even great tzaddikim in Eretz Yisrael cannot achieve such a cry from the depths.

Because malchus is the lowest level, Rosh Hashana, the day of malchus, is about bringing the kingship of Heaven down to the lowest place a Jew is in; this may be why Rosh Hashana has no aliyah l'regel to Yerushalayim.
Yosef left prison on Rosh Hashana to become ruler: whoever accepts the kingship of Heaven even in prison is himself the king and the free man.
The Rav reads 'shmitah to Hashem' as a mirror: by letting go of the debts others owe us, we cause Hashem to let go of the debt our sins have created.
Because the shmitah of years is counted from Tishrei, Rosh Hashanah is itself a time of release, and every Shabbos, the seventh day, is a small Rosh Hashanah with the same power.
Letzanus is the exact opposite of emunah: emunah is the gate into serving Hashem, and letzanus is the gate out of it.

Following Rabbi Tzadok, the Gemara's statement that scoffers do not receive the Shechinah means that the scoffer is kept out of the palaces of tefillah, so that even while davening his mind wanders elsewhere.
Pharaoh's superhuman stubbornness through the plagues came from his humor: a joke lets a person escape reality, so he never has to face it.
Pharaoh's punishment, 'that I made sport of Egypt', was measure for measure: Hashem let him make good jokes and then made a joke of him.
Just as the Torah was not satisfied with building cities of refuge but demanded signs at every crossroads, Elul does not help on its own: it must be announced and pointed out, or people pass it by.
Elul's verse, 'a road in the sea', describes a path that does not hold still: without constant signposts one drifts, and the forty days are gone before one notices.
One who truly relies only on Hashem is judged by Hashem alone and not by the lower courts, which explains the Arizal's promise that the sayer of L'Dovid emerges meritorious.
Following Rashi, the heart's stirring in Elul is itself Hashem's message, delivered through the heart as His messenger, telling a Jew to seek Him.

Every hour of the forty days is one lug of a mikveh; wasted hours are like drawn water poured in, and the remedy is to join oneself to Hashem, the true tzaddik, as a mikveh is repaired through contact with a kosher one.
Elul's own verse speaks of a killer, hinting that the teshuvah of Elul is for the 'bloodshed' of shaming and hurting another.
The word 'this' in 'this Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah expounded' is the finger of a generation that saw the Churban, pointing at sins between man and his fellow as its cause.

The Rav reads 'the place causes' of the rebellious elder as the meeting of the central soul with the central place: even the greatest sage of the Sanhedrin decides for all of Israel only when he sits where creation, and Torah, go out to the world.
The structure of the Torah mirrors creation: according to the Masorah, the middle pasuk of Sefer Devarim is the very pasuk of 'min hamakom hahu', from which 'the place causes' is learned.
Just as Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes, only the highest laws, those carrying kares, belong to the Great Sanhedrin in the highest place, while local matters stay with local courts.
The halachah books record the rashei teivos of Elul, something not done for other halachos, because a 'rosh' contains the whole word just as Rosh Hashanah contains the year.
The Avos are called mountains and were born in Tishrei because they are the small kernels from which the whole Jewish people grew, a point in time and in soul that holds much.

The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur parallel the forty days in which a child is formed: during them it is easy to pray that the year be blessed, while afterwards change is still possible but only with great effort.

The Rav reads bikkurim as a poel dimyoni: each of the seven species stands for a kind of Jew, so carrying them with music to the Mikdash enacts in advance the return of all Jews to Tziyon after the churban.

He counts back from the end of the Torah to show that the fiftieth praiseworthy mention of yetzias Mitzrayim is the bikkurim declaration, so the future geulah is tied to bikkurim and to the reading before Rosh Hashanah.
Since time is higher than place, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, the Mikdash of time, rise above the regalim of place, and no enemy, Bavel or Rome, could ever destroy them.
He explains the custom that the chazzan begins Hamelech from his place before reaching the amud: on Rosh Hashanah the King comes to each Jew, and he need not walk to the mizbeach.

Moshe instituted a prayer before prayer only on entering Eretz Yisroel, because only there did he feel a holiness greater than the heaven over chutz la'aretz; 'the heaven of heavens' in his praise is Eretz Yisroel.
The Rav defines life as freshness and death as aging; Adam's sin on Rosh Hashanah brought aging, and the Mikdash, where bread stayed warm and no one slept, is the place where that sin has no rule.
The fig that ripened before all others holds a soul of zrizus, so it belongs to the Mikdash, the place of reishis; this is why bikkurim, the first-ripened fruit, are brought there.

The Rav reads the Satan's flight to Botzrah as instinct, not reasoning: in sudden panic a being runs to its root, as the sea dog runs to dry land, so the flight itself reveals that Botzrah, the heart of Edom's harsh judgment, is his root.

Using the Yismach Moshe's rule that a gentile's unintentional act is at root deliberate, the Rav shows that the Satan's three 'errors' are not errors at all: fleeing to Botzrah reveals him as deliberate and therefore no angel protected by a refuge city.
The Rav connects the Kodesh HaKodashim, where no blemish enters, with the inner point of every Jew's heart where even the worst sinner never sinned, so Yerushalayim includes all the cities of refuge.

Since the mitzvah of three additional cities of refuge is the one mitzvah never fulfilled, the Rav sees it as Moshiach's own mitzvah, the one the Satan holds back, and which a Jew awakens when he runs to Hashem through Torah.
A murderer loses his place because he emptied the place of a person sent with a mission; by the same rule a Jew in galus has lost his place, and Yerushalayim, above place, gives it back.
The Rav links the Satan, whose name he connects with the number one hundred and with forgetting, to the hundred daily brachos, which are meant to keep a person remembering Hashem.

The souls of the very end, the forgotten and neglected ones, are bound to the very beginning, just as the last words of the Torah, 'le'einei kol Yisrael', are joined to Bereishis; in them lies the spark of Moshiach.

Moshe forgot the 1,775 shekels not as a lapse but because those Jews' very existence was shikchah: their half-shekel hung outside the Mishkan's curtain, so by Torah law they were 'to be forgotten', and Hashem, who never forgets, reminded him.
Haman's ten thousand talents redeemed only the half-shekels that became sockets; he thought he need pay nothing for the forgotten Jews, and that was his error.
Elul, like Adar, ends a half-year, and both are the time of hashavas aveidah: Dan the 'me'asef' and Esther, the lost one who is sought, are its souls, in contrast to Amalek who makes Jews lost.
The full spelling of the letters of kesef equals esh, the Rav says; so 'kesef malei' given by Avraham and Dovid was money with fire, while Haman's silver lacked it.
The numerical value of Yisrael minus that of Amalek is the value of esh: the whole difference between them is that Yisrael gives with fire and Amalek without it.

The Rav reads 'ki yipalei' as a matter belonging to the fiftieth gate, beyond the grasp of each tribe's judges, which is why it must go up to Yerushalayim, where 'the tribes went up' above their division.
Yaakov did not need to teach Yosef Taharos because Yosef, corresponding to Friday and Taharos, mastered it on his own, and this is the 'ben zekunim' for which Yaakov loved him more than his brothers.

Since tahara gives fruit its taste and smell, Yaakov sensed in the grain from Egypt the fragrance only Yosef, the order of Taharos, could put into it, and so 'saw that there was shever in Egypt', hope that Yosef lived.
Elul is not Yosef's month by the tribal banners, but it is by the seven shepherds; as the sixth, like Friday, it is Moshiach ben Yosef preparing for Tishrei, Moshiach ben David.
Elul has an advantage over Tishrei: like Shiloh, where kodashim were eaten wherever it was seen, it has no wall, and Yosef merited this open sanctity because he guarded his eyes.
Tzedakah, the midah of Yosef and yesod, draws down chesed that no other good deed can bring, because chesed is a free gift beyond what one deserves.
The place of the Mikdash is not stated in the Torah because it is not a place of nature: as the root point of creation it is hidden and can only be reached by seeking it.
Yerushalayim is the highest place not in elevation but because on a globe the 'top' is the point where its formation began.
The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur parallel the forty days in which a child is formed, so the year's formation is given into a person's hands through tefillah during them.
The middle verse of Sefer Devarim, about the Sanhedrin's ruling 'from that place', corresponds to the middle of the world, because the root of the Torah must sit in the root of creation.
Doeg's envy was not over a mere chiddush: by finding the place of the Mikdash, which is his own root, Dovid showed that he was the true king and not Shaul.
The Yamim Nora'im are named for the Beis HaMikdash, 'how awesome is this place', because they are the Mikdash in time.

The Rav reads the Chasam Sofer's explanation of hakhel as the way of Avraham rather than Chanoch: Chanoch withdrew and became like an angel, while Avraham gave up some of his own ascent to teach others, which is why Hashem praised Avraham, and why Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, who expounded the reward of bringing the children, is called Avraham's descendant.

The Rav draws a parallel between the king and Rosh Hashanah: as the king heads and includes the nation in the dimension of soul, Rosh Hashanah heads and includes the year in the dimension of time, so the head of the nation decides when the head of the year falls.

He answers his opening question by reading the order of the Mishnah as a statement: the chapter on a Rosh Hashanah 'sanctified by Heaven' precedes the shofar, because with the shofar one asks for a Rosh Hashanah and a king of revealed kingship, he'aras panim, not one of hidden face.

The Rav compares the infants at hakhel to every Jew at the shofar: the shofar speaks in thoughts too high for words that the mind does not grasp but the soul hears, just as the children absorb the king's words without understanding, and they may even receive what their grown parents no longer can.

He explains that the fear asked for on Rosh Hashanah is a fear of Hashem's goodness and majesty, 'mehadar geono', which for a Jew is the sweetest pleasure, the more fear the more delight, whereas a gentile only fears when something threatens him.

Through Hoshea the Rav shows why the Rosh Hashanah tears are tears of joy: Hashem told the prophet who suggested exchanging Israel that one cannot exchange a child, so the sinner who returns weeps as a child returning to his Father, with shame mixed with happiness.
Rosh Hashanah is like the factory where an item can be made exactly to order; during the year one is only at the store, where what was made can merely be redirected.
Daily tefillah can change the channel through which the blessing allotted on Rosh Hashanah flows, from wealth to children, but cannot add to its total.

Just as Yerushalayim is the place from which the world began, Rosh Hashanah is the Yerushalayim of the calendar; on the regalim Jews go up to the King, but on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur the King comes to every Jew.
Yerushalayim is a barren mother whose remembrance, like that of Sarah, Rachel and Chana, must come on Rosh Hashanah itself, and every Jew can be the one who brings it.
The commotion people make on earth is like a radio picking up waves from heaven, yet the nations' uproar over Eretz Yisrael is empty rebellion, and its only effect above is Hashem's laughter.
Because Rosh Hashanah is creation from nothing, only one who makes himself nothing can be created anew on it, which is why the more bent the shofar, the better.
'Teruah' means friendship: by joining with all of Klal Yisrael, as a fingernail shares in the body's good year, a person draws the judgment away from himself.

In the mashal the shofar is the merchant's advocate and Shabbos his relative: on a Shabbos Rosh Hashanah Shabbos defends the Jew, but only if he has not slighted it, so the Torah's 'no melachah' is advice to make peace with Shabbos.

The Torah, foreseeing the Rabbinic decree, gave 'zichron teruah' as a second path: since the shofar is withheld only for the sake of Shabbos, the withholding itself is a merit of Shabbos, and in the Mikdash, where there was no decree and so no such merit, the shofar had to be blown.

Shemittah frees a person from debts, and his greatest debts are sins; yovel, called by the shofar's own name, is a Shabbos of Shabbosos with the power of Yom Kippur, which is why one may confess between the tekios though sin is otherwise not mentioned on Rosh Hashanah.
Like the Gemara's teaching that refraining from praying for the sick on Shabbos itself brings healing, refraining from the shofar on Shabbos lets Shabbos itself have mercy and plead for the Jew.

Since Hashem created the world through ten utterances and ceased from them on Shabbos, the core of Shabbos observance for a refined Jew is ceasing from weekday speech, and even weekday thought, since the world was first conceived in thought.

The Rosh Hashanah readings speak only of Sarah and Chana being remembered and say nothing of judgment or creation, because the great barren one still awaiting remembrance is Yerushalayim; one should put her name in his prayers just as one asks a friend to pray for him.

The Rav, following the Arvei Nachal, reads 'all labor you shall not do' on Rosh Hashana that falls on Shabbos as Hashem's advice to appease Shabbos, which then pleads for Israel even more powerfully than the shofar.
Shabbos, as the day of the additional soul, is cast as a relative close to the Jewish soul who holds the highest office in the King's court, and before whom even the Satan trembles.
The Rav argues that because Hashem created the world with speech and thought, not with the hand, a ben Torah's rest on Shabbos must reach his speech and his thought.
Citing the Shelah, the Rav reads 'you shall call Shabbos a delight' as an obligation that Shabbos itself have pleasure from the person, not only that the person enjoy Shabbos.
The Rav explains that each verse of malchiyos, zichronos and shofaros is like one of the ten utterances, so the person saying it is creating the coming year's world, and himself along with it.
Since the final sealing extends to the last day of Chanukah, which this year falls on Shabbos, a person who has befriended Shabbos has an advocate even then.

The Mishnah places the story of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua just before the shofar chapter because it teaches that the nasi, the 'Rosh Hashanah of souls', fixes the Rosh Hashanah of time; the shofar chapter is then the acceptance of that King.

Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, a nasi appointed by Heaven through a miracle, darshened that children come to hakhel because his own root was a Father turning His face to His children; 'the generation is not orphaned' in which he lives.
Hakhel and Rosh Hashanah are parallel gatherings: hakhel gathers all souls, each a letter of the Torah, to the king who reads them; Rosh Hashanah gathers all days to their king.
A gentile who lacks something is afraid, but for a Jew it is the reverse: 'there is no lack for those who fear Him', for the one who lacks is the one without fear of Heaven.
Fear can be fear of goodness itself, as in 'they will fear Hashem and His goodness': one can be afraid of a gun or a wicked man, but the fear of Hashem's goodness is a sweet fear.

The tekios follow the Avos and David: tekiah, shevarim and teruah draw down Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov with David between them, and the tekiah gedolah is the shofar of Moshiach, the great hakhel of all souls.
The 'mishpat' of the G-d of Yaakov is read as the kal vachomer Yaakov can claim from Eisav: if Eisav's three tears won blessings, the tears of Yaakov's children must surely be answered.
The ram is not a substitute that lessens the akeidah but its completion: Avraham's longing to sacrifice joined to the deed of offering the ram, so the two are really one act.
The word 'itto' in 'nimolu itto' teaches that Avraham's longing to do the mitzvah again was joined to the circumcision of his household, so it counted as his own mitzvah more than once.
Moshe Rabbeinu cited the ram of the akeidah to ask that his longing not remain thought alone, and 'rav lach' answered that his longing was so great that no deed was needed.
'Kol hame'aneg es haShabbos' is read as one who gives delight to Shabbos, not one who takes pleasure on Shabbos.
Rosh Hashanah needs no aliyah l'regel because on it the quality of Yerushalayim, Hashem's kingship, comes out into the whole world, reaching even the Jews of chutz la'aretz.

When Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbos and the shofar is silent, the Shabbos itself takes the shofar's place as the Jews' advocate, so making peace with the Shabbos becomes the urgent avodah of Shabbos Shuva.
Since the esrog is like the heart, Hashem is the heart of Yisroel and Shabbos is His name, on a Shabbos when no lulav is taken the Shabbos itself serves as the Jews' esrog.
Shabbos is one sixtieth of Olam Haba, yet unlike a forbidden taste that is nullified in sixty, its taste of Olam Haba can still be felt if one prepares for it.
Hashem gave Moshe a third sign so as not to rule between Rebbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on chazakah, because the Written Torah does not decide disputes of the Oral Torah.
In Haazinu one ushpiz of a disputed day is named explicitly and the other only hinted, so that the Torah does not decide between the Arizal's order and the other order of the ushpizin.
The last pasuk of Haazinu, the 122nd from Rosh Chodesh Elul, corresponds to Zos Chanukah: one may look at the hidden light but not yet use it, as Moshe could see the land but not enter.
The Rav reads 'a way in the sea' as a way through a sea of sins: sins that block a person from holiness like a sea are given a path in Elul.
The four words of 'Ani ledodi vedodi li' each end in a yud, together forty, the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur, the days the second luchos were made for those who had sinned.
The mikveh of the forty days is completed only at the very end of Yom Kippur, matching the final mishnah of Yoma, 'Mikveh Yisrael Hashem'.
Each Shabbos meal belongs to one of the Avos, so one who sits at the meal with seriousness and pure thoughts has the holy Avos with him.
The bas kol calling to teshuvah sounds every day but only a pure heart hears it; in Elul the days themselves cry out, so even one whose hearing is dulled can hear.
Learning Tomer Devorah, which teaches how to practice the Thirteen Attributes between man and his fellow, is itself a way to arouse them in Elul.

The Rav reads 'har' of the Beis Hamikdash as related to conception: the Mikdash is the first point from which everything develops, like an embryo from its first point, and is therefore called the place of thought.

He maps the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur onto the forty days of a child's formation: within them one can still pray for a year of blessing, while after Yom Kippur it is like a prayer said too late.
Because Adam HaRishon was created on Rosh Hashanah from the place of the Mikdash, the roots of place, time and soul meet in him, and Rosh Hashanah is a seed whose flaw carries through the whole year.

Every root point is hidden and needs seeking: David, the soul of Adam, was overlooked among Yishai's sons; the place of the Mikdash was mistaken at first; and Rosh Hashanah is covered even from the angels.
What the Mikdash is in place, the king is in the soul: both are the heart, which is why David, the root of malchus, was the one who found the place of the Mikdash.

Since the world mirrors the Torah, Jerusalem at the center of the world must have a counterpart at the center of the Torah, and the Rav finds it in the middle verse of Sefer Devarim, which sends halachah to 'the place'.

The knocking of the Avos in these days is explained as a meeting of two roots: the Avos are the root of every Jewish soul, and the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah, corresponding to the ten utterances of creation, are the root of the year, so when the root of time arrives the root of the soul stirs.

Yom Kippur is the one day of 'echad' because yechidah is the level where all Jewish souls fuse, as in Yaakov Avinu before the tribes divided; therefore hatred toward another Jew is a barrier to the day itself, not only a separate sin.

The precious stone the tailor found in his fish is read as the seven blessings of the Yom Kippur Shemoneh Esrei: the fish, a creature that stayed pure before the Mabul, gave him sparks of righteousness that let him daven a true Yom Kippur prayer.
The word for tailor is taken as an image of Yom Kippur: a tailor takes separate cut pieces and joins them into one garment, and a Jew's success on Yom Kippur is fitting himself into that unity.

The sealing at Ne'ilah is the engraving of the second luchos on each Jewish heart, cut as deep as the heart was softened through teshuvah, so the real 'good sealing' is a heart for avodas Hashem all year.

On Yom Kippur Jews do eat: they eat the mann in its original angelic form, the food Moshe ate on the mountain, so the fast is itself the oneg Shabbos and the greater the affliction, the greater the delight.
Kol Nidrei opens Yom Kippur because, as Rabbah bar bar Chana's story hints, the vow to annul is Hashem's own oath to keep Israel in galus.
Just as the Beis HaMikdash is a mountain in place rising to the holy of holies, the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul are a mountain in time, and Yom Kippur at Ne'ilah is its holy of holies.

The pesukim of the season's parshiyos match the levels of teshuvah: Vayeilech's thirty for those who walk ahead, Nitzavim's forty for those who stand still, Ha'azinu's fifty-two for those who need until Shemini Atzeres, and together 122, the days to Zos Chanukah.
When Yom Kippur falls on Shabbos, the Shabbos is strengthened by Yom Kippur and the day is compounded, so its kapparah is greater than that of an ordinary Yom Kippur.
Dividing the sixth millennium into twenty-four 'hours' of about 250 years, the Rav shows that 5751 enters the midday of the world's Erev Shabbos, when one may already begin to prepare for Shabbos.

Rabbi Yaakov Kamenetsky's remark that Shabbos was brought back in America but Erev Shabbos was not becomes, for the Rav, the key to the world's Erev Shabbos: as a Jew honors Erev Shabbos below, Heaven begins the Shabbos of the world.

Through the Tiferes Shlomo, the Rav reads 'the last generation will say' as a description of whoever cries out: the generation that demands of Hashem why strangers hold Eretz Yisroel becomes the last generation of the galus.
The crown that Jews' tefillos make for the King of Glory is the very crown that will rest on Moshiach's head, so it is up to Jews now to 'hammer out' that crown.

The Rav concedes that the Tzedukim's reasoning about honoring a king seems correct, and locates their error not in the halachah but in their view of the relationship: before a King one prepares outside, but a wife cooks freely in her husband's presence.

He ties the Tzedukim's denial of the Oral Torah to the ketores: the Chachamim are the akeres habayis who run the house of Torah, and whoever denies them also denies that Klal Yisroel is Hashem's wife and sees Him only as a King.

In the Rosh Hashanah Shemoneh Esrei Klal Yisroel speaks to Hashem, as subjects to a king; the novelty of the Yom Kippur Shemoneh Esrei is that Hashem speaks to Klal Yisroel with affection, as a husband to his wife.
Because smell alone was not damaged in the sin of the Etz HaDaas, the ketores expresses a love untouched by any sin; fittingly, the Tzeduki who denied that love was punished in his nose.
Shir HaShirim, a short megillah said before Mincha on Erev Shabbos, is full of fragrances from its first verses to its last, which shows that it is the same matter as the ketores.
In kedushah, unlike tumah which is separation, love and fear can exist together; the fear of Rosh Hashanah is a fear born of love.
